entities.name: Guillaume de la Sudrie
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guillaume de la Sudrie (d. 1373), a French Dominican friar from Laguenne, Corrèze, rose through the ecclesiastical hierarchy to become a cardinal and a significant figure during the Avignon Papacy. His career, spanning the mid-14th century, saw him navigate the complex political and religious landscape of Western Europe, demonstrating the influence of mendicant orders within the Church and their capacity to shape papal policy and administration. His elevation to cardinal by Pope Urban V in 1366 underscores his perceived loyalty and competence in a period marked by attempts to reform the Church and restore the papacy to Rome.

Beginning his service as Bishop of Marseille in early 1361, Guillaume de la Sudrie administered a strategically vital Mediterranean diocese, a gateway for trade and crusader movements. His elevation to Cardinal-Priest of Santi Giovanni e Paolo by Urban V on September 18, 1366, placed him within the inner circle of the College of Cardinals. He actively participated in the papal court at Avignon, serving as a trusted advisor and holding key positions. Notably, he was a member of the commission appointed by Urban V to inquire into the accusations against the English Franciscan Adam Easton in 1369, showcasing his involvement in doctrinal and disciplinary matters at the highest level of the Church.

De la Sudrie's influence extended to the curial efforts to manage the Hundred Years' War and the ongoing schism within the Holy Roman Empire, as well as the initial attempts to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome. His participation in the conclave of 1370, which elected Pope Gregory XI, solidified his role in shaping the future direction of the Church during a tumultuous era. Although his death in 1373 predated the Great Western Schism, his career exemplifies the late medieval Church's centralized power structure and the pivotal role of cardinals in its governance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guillaume de la Sudrie was a significant cardinal during the Avignon Papacy, contributing to the administration and diplomatic efforts of the Church, including the election of Pope Gregory XI who returned the papacy to Rome. His career exemplifies the ascent of mendicant friars to high office and their influence on papal policy in the 14th century.
